scope: Security review of policy_compiler v3 (C++ engine, server.py bridge, index.html console). Findings marked 'live' were reproduced by running the real binary; 'source' were confirmed by scanning the source; 'review' come from reading the code only.
notes: No part of the engine calls an LLM or the network: the 'agents' are deterministic rule code. Prompt-injection defences therefore protect against a future LLM integration, and the real attack surface today is the policy text turning into generated code, plus the local web server.

items.title: Code injection into generated Python / TypeScript / JSON validators
items.what: forbidWord strings are pasted into the generated source with no escaping (the C++ target does escape them through cEscape; the other three targets do not). A policy line such as forbidWord "x', __import__('os').system('id')]#" becomes executable Python.
items.impact: Whoever can influence a policy file gets code execution on every machine that runs the generated validator. The web console is protected only because the AI Guard happens to flag the quote characters; the CLI (--emit-all) runs with the guard OFF unless --guard is passed.
items.fix: Escape per target language (json.dumps for Python and JSON, a JS string escaper for TypeScript), and restrict forbidWord to an allow-list such as [A-Za-z0-9 _-] in the semantic stage. Make the guard on by default.

items.title: Hard-coded signing key and a home-made 'HMAC'
items.what: The 'HMAC Integrity Signature' is sha256(key:sha256(key:data)) with the fixed key "agentic_policy_salt_2026" compiled into the program and shipped in the repository. It is not the standard HMAC construction.
items.impact: Anyone with the source can compute a valid signature for any tampered policy, so the signature proves nothing about integrity or origin.
items.fix: Use real HMAC-SHA256 with a per-deployment secret from the environment or a key store, or sign with an asymmetric scheme (Ed25519) and verify inside the generated validator.

items.title: AI Guard is a phrase blocklist and is easy to bypass
items.what: Detection relies on fixed phrases, a Cyrillic-only look-alike map and keyword heuristics. A paraphrase scores 0.00 and is allowed outright. Fullwidth letters, Greek look-alikes, soft hyphens and other languages are not normalised. A single rule hit has weight 0.55, below the 0.60 BLOCK threshold, so it only warns and compilation continues.
items.impact: The project's own attack simulation shows 25% attack success with the guard on. Real attackers will find the other 75% easy to rephrase.
items.fix: Treat the policy language as a strict grammar: reject any line that is not a valid rule or a comment, and never interpret comment text. Normalise with full Unicode NFKC and strip all format characters. Make WARN on a bypass phrase a BLOCK.

items.title: Local web server has no authentication, Host check or Origin check
items.what: Any web page open in the user's browser can send requests to http://127.0.0.1:8000. A request with Host: attacker.example and Origin: http://evil.example is answered with 200. DNS rebinding turns this into full read access.
items.impact: A malicious site can run compiles, trigger the attack simulation (which writes to attacks.log), read the attack log and submit passwords to the evaluator.
items.fix: Reject requests whose Host is not localhost:8000 or 127.0.0.1:8000, require a random per-run token in a custom header, and send no CORS headers.

items.title: Single-threaded server with no timeouts: one stalled request freezes it
items.what: HTTPServer handles one connection at a time and has no socket timeout. The body is read with int(Content-Length) before the 65,000-character cap is applied, so a client that announces a body and never sends it blocks every other request. A lying or negative length is not validated.
items.impact: Denial of service for the console from any local process or web page; confirmed by hand with a half-open request (the next request timed out).
items.fix: Use ThreadingHTTPServer, set a per-connection timeout, and reject Content-Length above a small limit before reading.

items.title: noUserInfo is silently not enforced when no username is supplied
items.what: With noUserInfo true and an empty username, a password containing the user's name is accepted and reported as valid. The engine knows it skipped the check (userCheckSkipped) but the result does not say so.
items.impact: A policy that looks stricter than it is; accounts can end up with name-based passwords.
items.fix: Fail closed: refuse to evaluate, or mark the result as 'not verified', when noUserInfo is set and no username is given.

items.title: Entropy estimator over-rates passwords built from unlisted words
items.what: Only words in the small built-in list are priced as dictionary hits; everything else is charged as random characters. Name + symbol + year passwords therefore score as very strong.
items.impact: minEntropy gives false assurance. 'Tr0ub4dor&3xx' scores about 85 bits and 'MyDogRocky#2023' about 79 bits, although both are guessable with simple rules.
items.fix: Load a large breached-password and word list (100k+ entries) and score with a zxcvbn-style matcher; cap the score for dictionary-plus-suffix patterns.

items.title: attacks.log grows without limit and is trusted by the viewer
items.what: Every flagged request appends a line to attacks.log in the working directory. There is no rotation or size cap, and the server joins raw lines into a JSON array without validating them.
items.impact: An unauthenticated caller (see V-04) can fill the disk; one malformed line breaks the log viewer.
items.fix: Rotate or cap the file, rate-limit logging, and parse each line before returning it.

items.title: Windows random-number fallback may be predictable
items.what: If CryptGenRandom fails, the code falls back to std::random_device, although the comment says it never uses a weak generator. On older MinGW toolchains std::random_device is deterministic.
items.impact: Generated passwords could be reproducible on affected Windows builds. Not tested here (Linux only).
items.fix: Use BCryptGenRandom and abort on failure, as the Linux branch already does.

items.title: Integrity check in generated validators only detects table edits
items.what: The embedded fingerprint is a plain SHA-256 of the policy table. An attacker who edits the table can edit the fingerprint too. FEATURES.md already says this.
items.impact: The check stops accidents, not tampering. Combine with a real signature (see V-02).
items.fix: Verify an asymmetric signature over the policy table at start-up.
